text: Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn calibrate a confidence radius by inverting a concentration bound. They recommend bootstrap or cross-validation in practice because the a priori bound can be conservative. This recommendation does not itself establish a dependence-aware coverage theorem. (low confidence)

Li’s Wasserstein-Kelly concentration result requires independently drawn observations and a light-tailed distribution. Its statistical guarantee must retain those assumptions when used to calibrate a radius. (low confidence)

For independent, identically distributed observations and the specified exponential-tail assumption, Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn calibrate a Wasserstein radius by inverting a concentration bound at a prescribed failure probability. Their resulting ambiguity ball is a confidence set for the true distribution and yields a finite-sample out-of-sample cost bound. The concentration theorem reproduced in the Wasserstein-Kelly paper likewise explicitly requires independent samples and a light-tail condition; applying this route to dependent financial returns requires a separately justified result. (medium confidence)

Duchi, Glynn and Namkoong provide an alternative based on smooth f-divergence balls. Their dependent-data theorem for an aperiodic, positive Harris recurrent Markov chain requires sufficiently fast beta-mixing, Lipschitz and loss moment bounds, and a unique optimizer. Its coverage limit depends on the ratio of marginal loss variance to long-run loss variance, with the latter including lagged covariances. Thus an IID chi-square calibration cannot simply be carried over unchanged to serially dependent observations. The result is asymptotic coverage for the optimal objective, not finite-sample Wasserstein-ball coverage. (low confidence)

Blanchet, Kang and Murthy calibrate uncertainty using robust Wasserstein profile inference: find the minimum transport cost needed to make an estimating equation hold, then use a confidence-level quantile of that profile to make the population-optimal parameter plausible. This targets a confidence region for an optimal parameter rather than requiring coverage of the entire true distribution. Their general setup assumes IID observations, and their practical quantile approximation uses asymptotic analysis; Gao explicitly identifies the asymptotic limitation of this approach. (medium confidence)

Gao develops non-asymptotic, loss-sensitive Wasserstein DRO guarantees using concentration controlled by loss variation and localized Rademacher complexity. The analysis relates radius selection to Lipschitz or gradient variation instead of only full-distribution coverage. Its setup uses IID samples and distributional concentration assumptions, including transportation-information inequalities; it is not a general certificate for heavy-tailed, serially dependent Kelly returns. (low confidence)

A radius chosen to cover the entire data-generating distribution can be conservative in moderate or high dimension. Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn recommend bootstrap or cross-validation calibration in practice, while Gao distinguishes this distribution-coverage approach from guarantees adapted to the loss family. Practical tuning should therefore state which guarantee it targets, rather than equating good validation performance with distribution coverage. (medium confidence)

Keehan, Anderson and Wiesemann calibrate Wasserstein ambiguity balls around weighted empirical distributions to balance sampling variability against bounded distribution drift. Their concentration theorem assumes bounded support, a bound on successive infinity-Wasserstein shifts, and independent observations. The resulting radius reflects both effective sample size and accumulated drift. The paper explicitly retains independence to focus on drift, so recency weighting here does not itself solve serial-dependence calibration. (low confidence)

Long proposes block multiplier bootstrap validation of a finite menu of Wasserstein-DRO CVaR portfolios. The preprint’s abstract describes a probability bound without an asymptotic remainder, while its conditional theorem includes a vanishing remainder. Treat this as an attributed CVaR validation proposal, not an established exact finite-sample Kelly guarantee. (low confidence)

In its diversification experiment, the Wasserstein-Kelly paper sets the ambiguity radius as a multiple of the average log return across assets and varies that proportion. This is an experimental radius parameterization, distinct from a procedure that inverts a concentration bound to certify a prescribed coverage level; its separate statistical theorem requires independent light-tailed draws. (low confidence)
Qingyun Sun’s public repository lists a Kelly optimization notebook. (low confidence)

Sun and Boyd define distributionally robust Kelly betting as maximizing the smallest expected log growth over a given set of probability distributions. Their finite-outcome tractability result supplies fixed-set context; it does not by itself select a statistical coverage level or a data-calibrated set size. (low confidence)

Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn give a concrete holdout procedure: solve the robust optimization problem for a finite grid of radii using training data, evaluate the resulting decisions by sample-average loss on validation data, and choose a radius minimizing that validation loss. Their k-fold variant averages the radii selected in separate holdout runs and refits on all samples. These procedures are presented within their IID sampling framework. (low confidence)

For the same dependent-data setting, Duchi, Glynn and Namkoong propose sectioning observations into consecutive blocks, computing robust optimal values within blocks, and studentizing the block results. Their proposition obtains pivotal Student-t asymptotics under the preceding theorem’s conditions. This is a justified block-based inference method with an asymptotic guarantee; it does not establish arbitrary block-bootstrap validity or finite-sample Kelly leverage calibration. (low confidence)

The Wasserstein-Kelly paper warns that a naive Wasserstein ambiguity ball for simple returns can admit negative portfolio gross returns outside the logarithm’s domain; even a nonnegative-support constraint can leave its worst-case expectation unbounded. The authors instead formulate ambiguity over log returns. For Kelly calibration, the modeled uncertainty variable and admissible support therefore need specification before a radius has a meaningful interpretation. (low confidence)
